newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria plunges into petrol shortage.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria plunges into petrol shortage.

text.p: Debt-ridden Bulgaria has added a fuel shortage to its economic problems due to a lack of cash for crude supplies, officials said on Wednesday.
"The problem is that there is no crude in the Bourgas refinery," said Petar Tsanov, deputy director of the biggest state-owned fuel retailer, Petrol.
Petrol's 450 filling stations are running short of fuel. Those which are still open are distributing their last drops.
"The situation is becoming disastrous. Bulgarians will need bicycles," Tsanov told Reuters.

Shell Bulgaria, a Royal Dutch/Shell group subsidiary and the only foreign fuel retailer in Bulgaria, said all its four petrol stations in Sofia had closed due to a lack of fuel. Its remaining 23 stations in the country do not have all kinds of gasoline.
"Neftohim's fate defines our fate as we are dependant on the refinery," said Shell spokeswoman Kamelia Slaveikova.
The Neftohim refinery in Bourgas is Shell's only gasoline supplier in Bulgaria. The retailer does not plan to import any gasoline for its stations as customs fees are high, she said.
Neftohim said it has been refining only 8,000 tonnes of crude per day since Monday, down from 16,000 tonnes last week.
The refinery, which posted losses of 100 billion levs last year and 37 billion levs in January, has closed down one distillation unit and another one is close to its minimum.
Gasoline deliveries on Tuesday totalled 1,000 tonnes and the plant has distributed 2,000 tonnes of diesel oil and 3,000 tonnes of naphtha, plant spokeswoman Tatyana Hadzhieva said.
She said a 72,000-tonne crude tanker was expected to arrive at Bourgas later on Wednesday from Russia's port of Odessa.

However, officials said that one tanker could provide some petrol for 4-5 days but could not solve the country's gasoline shortage as it was unclear whether any oil supplier would deliver crude to a bankrupt refinery.
Russia's state-owned Rosneft oil company said on Tuesday it had cut crude oil supplies to Neftohim because of unpaid debts.
Neftohim's management has complained many times of low domestic prices as it says the plant now meets almost 100 percent of the country's fuel needs.
The 31-year-old plant purchases its crude at international spot market prices in hard currency while domestic fuel prices are several times lower than production costs, refinery officials say.
Energy officials said the new petrol and diesel fuel prices, to be raised by 48 percent on the average from Thursday, will not help Neftohim as one litre of petrol would be sold for some 14 cents.
The government revises energy prices monthly in line with the inflation rate, the lev/dollar exchange rate and world oil prices.
